newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania urged to replant to revive coffee output.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania urged to replant to revive coffee output.

text.p: Extensive and immediate replanting is needed in Tanzania's coffee areas to halt a sharp decline in output, senior industry officials and traders said.
Jeremy Lefroy, managing director of Moshi-based Africa Coffee Co, said most of the coffee trees in key northern growing zone should be uprooted.

"The only way for Tanzania's coffee to recover is by increasing production to at least 60,000 tonnes, where it was before...and the only way to increase production is through replanting," Lefroy told Reuters.
He called for private buyers to become directly involved in providing seedlings.
Edward Sannda, Tanzania Coffee Board Managing Director, has forecast production in the current 1996/97 season at between 41,000 and 43,000 tonnes, worth an estimated $90 million.
This would compare with 1995/96 output of 53,000 tonnes which earned about $115 million, and around 44,000 tonnes in 1994/95, worth $139 million.

"I reckon we need somewhere in the vicinity of five million seedlings a year and we are not even doing 500,000," Lefroy said, adding that output in the south would slump from 18,000 tonnes in 1995/96 to 12,0000 in 1996/97.
He forecast northern production at 15,000-16,000 tonnes in 1996/97 from 21,500 in 1995/96.
Mild arabica coffee from the northern zone surrounding Mount Kilimanjaro comprises about 50 percent of Tanzania's arabica production, which accounts for 75 percent of total output.
The only area where production was holding up was western Bukoba, Tanzania's main robusta growing region, he said.
"The key issue is to get private buyers to get involved in the rehabilitation of the trees," he said.

He said that was not an easy task and would only occur if buyers were legally required to get involved. "My view is that replanting is justified on its own merits. The yield in Tanzania is one of the lowest in the world."
Average yields were given by the coffee board as 200-300 kg per hectare.
Sannda said he backed Lefroy's call. "The biggest requirement is the replacement of old trees," Sannda told Reuters.
"Most trees are between 50 to 100 years. Those trees should be uprooted -- slowly, of course, because you must have a plan, and you should uproot in stages," he added.

Sannda predicted resistance from many smallholders due to temporary loss of income. But he said there was no alternative to replanting and that a phased scheme would soften the economic impact on smallholders.
Industry analysts said coffee trees attained maximum output at between seven and 20 years, after which regular pruning could sustain commercial production until about 40 years.
